children: Microsoft
expects revenue and Azure growth to accelerate in the December quarter as delayed AI infrastructure spending shifts into the second half of the fiscal year.
The company guided for
Q2 revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion
, above analysts' estimate of about $95.6 billion.
Azure growth is expected to reach
49% to 50% in constant currency
, up from 48% in the September quarter.
That matters because investors had initially focused on Microsoft's lower-than-expected capital spending.
Q1 capital expenditures came in at
$45.2 billion
, with CFO Amy Hood explaining that some third-party capacity deliveries expected during the quarter were delayed.
Those costs have not disappeared.
Microsoft now expects
Q2 CapEx to exceed $50 billion
, while calendar-year spending is projected at roughly
$170 billion
as delayed capacity moves into later quarters.
Management also stressed that demand remains stronger than available supply.
Hood said some third-party GPU-as-a-Service contracts have shifted into the second half, while new capacity additions and engineering efficiencies could create quarterly variability in Azure growth.
The underlying business remains strong.
Q1 revenue reached
$92.3 billion
, up 19% year over year and ahead of analysts' expectations. EPS came in at
, compared with the $4.72 consensus.
Microsoft Cloud revenue topped
$63 billion
, growing 30%, while Azure increased 48%.
The company also continues to expand its AI platform.
Foundry revenue more than tripled year over year, while Microsoft now has more than
120,000 Foundry customers
. Paid Fabric customers climbed above 44,000, up more than 50%.
Copilot usage also accelerated, with daily users up nearly 50% sequentially and customers using consumption-based credits rising more than 75%.
Investor Takeaway
I think the biggest takeaway is that Microsoft's capex miss looks much more like a
timing issue than a weakening AI demand signal
That distinction is important.
Management says customer demand still exceeds supply, Azure growth is accelerating toward 50%, and the infrastructure spending that missed Q1 is now moving into Q2 and the second half.
For investors, the more important question is whether Microsoft can convert that enormous spending into sustained revenue growth without sacrificing margins.
So far, the numbers remain impressive.
Operating margin held around
, while free cash flow reached
$18.6 billion
despite the heavy investment cycle.
The key things to watch are
Azure growth, CapEx deployment, Copilot consumption, Foundry adoption and whether delayed third-party capacity comes online on schedule
Microsoft is not backing away from AI infrastructure.
It is preparing to spend even more.

title: Microsoft Stock Gets Surprising AI Spending Reality Check
